utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, have you had time to rest a little? I appreciate the fact that during the war you were wounded and that you are ill and I shall try during the afternoon to be as specific as possible, so that we could make the examination easier. Before the break, we talked about a document which was submitted to you for review, 27th of July, 1992, was the date. To clarify certain facts, I would like to ask you, Mr. Cerovac, according to the regulations and the armed forces, who composed the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina? According to this regulation the formation of Bosnia and Herzegovina were the TO, the HVO and the MUP and the forces of the interior. Regardless of the orders you have seen, on the basis of your own experience in the municipal staff of Konjic, did Mr. Delalic as commander of TG-1 have ever become a superior authority over the TO and the HVO and the MUP in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never, neither in theory, nor in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you followed a group of members of the TO during the JUG operation. Mr. Cerovac, is it true that part of the forces, and from Konjic, was subordinated to Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I led such a group, personally. It was about 150 soldiers so that parts of the forces of Konjic were subordinated for certain Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have some evidence and I would like to show the witness document T 146/1. I would like this document to be placed on the ELMO, so that the judges can see it. Can the document be seen? Have you seen the document earlier on, Mr. Cerovac? Have another look. Put -- please put the English version on the ELMO. The English version, thank you. And you look through the Bosnian version, please. Mr. Cerovac, is this document signed by the President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On this document, has it been clearly indicated that Mr. Delalic was commander of TG-1 in the upper part of this order, in the preamble, you can see the official gazette on the basis of which orders are issued. Is it indisputable that Mr. Delalic was commander of TG-1? Can you see this from the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's nothing questionable here, it was clearly indicated that Mr. Delalic was commander of TG-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Has it ever been disputable? Has been this appointment been ever a question of dispute for you? And after his appointment, did you know that Mr. Delalic was only commander of TG-1 and that he had no other responsibilities or authority? Was that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may be an issue of interpretation. On page 59, line 14, the answer to the question on the LiveNote is "No." I believe the witness said "Yes." Could that be verified, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that President Izetbegovic signed it, so the mistake was in the transcript, it relates to the appointment. It was nothing, it was only a mistake in the transcript. The appointment was, in fact, signed by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a mistake in the transcript. Mr. Cerovac, were you personally ever been a member of the Tactical Group 1 command? Were you, Mr. Cerovac, at any point in time in 1992, were you a soldier of TG-1 that is subordinate to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, were the guards of the prison, were they soldiers or subordinates to the commander of TG-1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, we are discussing the issue of the tactical group. Mr. Cerovac, do you know whether the guards or the personnel of the Celebici camp subordinated to the coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, you said that Goran Lokas was president of the military investigation committee. Tell me, do you know that at the beginning of June, Mr. Lokas had a traffic accident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went to the Republic of Croatia and since he was absent for some time, we were informed, Mr. Dinko Zebic told me, personally, that he had had a car accident. I don't know about the details, I was not told about the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the position of the deputy for security in the joint command belonged to the HVO, do you know if someone had been appointed to the post, earlier occupied by Mr. Lokas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Jerko Kostic in the premises of the joint command. Actually in the offices where Mr. Lokas used to work, it was a person whom I had known before the aggression and who worked in the security service of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When we talked about the commission, although you had mentioned that it was not part of your job, but as a member of the joint command, did you know what the task of the commission was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to say the following in response to your question. In my training, I have never been in a position to work on matters of military investigation and I am familiar with those techniques and you can draw the conclusion that I am not familiar with the techniques of interrogation, examination and so forth. In the joint command, that is what I know, we wrote out some orders which referred to the work, which related to the work of the commission, which dealt with correctness of the procedure itself, not to use coercive measures and so on. And we had drawn up such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now you said that you had done this with regard to the work of the commission, in the joint command in the TO staff. Did one pay heed to legal procedures and to the respect of human rights of civilians in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we paid heed to that, especially some orders, which we had issued related to the protection of the civilian population, especially population of the Serb nationality, who lived on the territory of the Konjic municipality. In fact, with regard to their personal protection with regard to not appropriating their property, their cattle and not mistreating them and so on. And even in these orders, we had organised certain points. Actually, we had written out certain points, relating to tasks of protection of the Serb population, and we appointed responsible persons to take care of that. I think that I have mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you three documents and I would like to ask you whether you are familiar with these documents and if you had perhaps drawn them up yourself, can you tell the judges that? Please show the witness document 245 A5, D-20. Exhibit 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How are these documents relevant to command responsibility? The staff, the TO is not before us. I have seen some documents issued, even the declaration of war, issued by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, contains a specific paragraph in that regard, how does that effect us in solving the question of command responsibility, so far as your client is concerned? You're just wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, Article 7, whoever is -- I am talking about command responsibility -- whoever was in command, did or did not take the necessary measures to punish the perpetrators. These are documents which relate to the fact that, whether the command had tried to prevent something or not and that is how I understand Article 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The article has nothing to do with Celebici camp. He was not in charge, he had no relations with that camp. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is the command in these particular circumstance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These instructions have not been issued by him, they've been issued by the State and the functions of the State. Let's confine ourselves to the responsibility of your client. You've already led evidence to show that he's not a member of the TO, he's not a member of the war presidency and he's not a member of the MUP. And as a TG-1 commander, he had no responsibility of this Celebici prison. Even when he was made commander of all the formations, that did not include Celebici camp for the reason that he had a specific task of leaving the -- but that's enough. Why are you going into these areas, they're not relevant for your purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you had listened to the witness, he was talking about something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be enough...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's been held responsible for the acts of others. But he says your defence is that he had nothing to do with those persons, as a commander. That's your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So why are we going into all these matters? Yours is a very specific and limited task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is clear, then you should ask the Prosecutor. As long as such an indictment exists, we must cast this doubt on every element of the indictment and not only what we are saying, what is clear to me and to you, seems not to be clear to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are so many accused, charged with different offences. Yours is a limited one, command responsibility. You're being held vicariously responsible for the acts of the others and you say that I had nothing to do with those persons who committed those acts and this is your case. So that should be the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But only on the basis of the indictment, he said that he was responsible for everything according to the prosecution. So you should not adopt this attitude. I would like to point to some facts that are quite contrary to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The evidence now which you are relying upon, is evidence of another tactical Group 2, but not of Group 1. So it doesn't have any relevance to what he could have done, even if he did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the forces from Konjic was under somebody else's responsibility rather than Delalic's, isn't that something significant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's -- in the JUP. Your case is, as I understand, that he had nothing as commander of TG-1 or assistant chief of staff in the JUP, he had nothing to do with the salvaging camp, so that should be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is what we claim and what we are proving, but for us to be able to prove that fully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Bosnia Government of regard to observation, be relevant in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We spend so much time on a very simple matter. It's this witness that you have been examining and he has told you what he did. And I don't see how you link it with your defence. He's told you what he did and what happened in the group, in which he worked. Well, if you want to share that, share it. But I don't see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's provided in the -- the armed forces would be what the Geneva convention is about and this is exactly what the Bosnia government has done and what the functions of the Bosnia government has done. And right in the convention themselves, that the armed forces would be taught, given lessons in regard to the provisions at the Geneva convention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, life was far more complicated than this case itself. And I am trying to illustrate a part of that life for you. If you feel that is not necessary, the document that were part of the supporting material of the expert witness indicate the order to strictly respect the Geneva conventions. And whoever participated, discharged his duties in the way assigned to him. It is hard to explain that a country one day old swept by war. It is very difficult to explain what happened and I don't know how you will understand this camp if you don't know the rest. But anyway, that is not up to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, could you tell me whether you know anything about who had the authority to release prisoners from the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The knowledge I had at the time was as follows: A part of the prisoners were released by the military investigations commission. Then, the prisoners were released when somebody intervened on their behalf, people with prestige from Konjic. Also, through certain family connections, there were family links. There was intermarriage between Croats, Muslims and Serbs, so there were family links too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, while you were standing in for Commander Ramic, were you ever consulted regarding the release of any of the prisoners from Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this occurred in the second half of July and on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what happened, if you can remember, in the first case, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall very briefly, not to take up the time of their Honours and all of you here present. The first time it occurred was upon the intervention of Mr. Tahirovic. Actually, it was a friend of his, whom I knew personally, because we were of the same generation and his name was Miro Golubovic. And the communication was between Konjic and Glavaticevo, which is about 15 or 16 kilometres, as the crow flies. And the situation in Konjic at the time was highly tense. There was anti-Serb feeling was rampant because, in July, a mysterious killing occurred, of a TO policeman in the Village of Bradina. Or more precisely, Duboki Potok. So that animosity soared. That is how I understood Mr. Tahirovic. So there was no communication between us for a long time. Not to keep the lines engaged and not to allow the enemy to listen in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, after being informed by Mr. Tahirovic about this anti-Serb feeling, and after his intervention on behalf of his friend, Golubovic, did you undertake anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I told Tahirovic that he should find the necessary forms and to try, by messenger, to send them to the Glavaticevo region where I was situated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did those forms reach you at Glavaticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not those forms, because in the surroundings of Glavaticevo and in Glavaticevo itself, the situation was extremely difficult in the combat sense. There were casualties whom we had to take care of, so that I was told that the messenger had reached Vranske Stijene, whereas I, due to the situation in which I was and the events in the surroundings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You didn't ask him to go into those details. You only asked him what did he do in regards to Tahirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The release of documents, I think that's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, did you authorise anyone -- you have explained why you, yourself, didn't receive those documents. Did you give anyone to sign on your behalf this document for Miro Golubovic? The court wants you to be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Delalic told me that this messenger had arrived with these forms in connection with Miro Golubovic, so I told him to sign it because the messenger could not go on foot for six or seven hours. The messenger was not in a position to be able to do that. I had other more pressing business. There were dead people. There were wounded people, so I told him to sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, while performing your duties as staff commander, did you, on any other occasion, authorise Mr. Delalic to sign a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This also happened while I was at Glavaticevo. This was maybe four, five, six days after this contact with Mr. Tahirovic and the case with Mr. Golubovic. Dr. Izetbegovic contacted me in connection with the case of two doctors, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in connection with that conversation, know that Mr. Delalic was there present with Dr. Ahmar Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Izetbegovic said that. He said that he was speaking over his Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then, while acting as commander of the municipal staff, authorise somebody to be able to sign the discharge papers after these requests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As in the first case, I decided quickly and said that Mr. Zejnil Delalic should do that, and I concentrated on my own business.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, do you know whether other persons, for instance, the head of the MUP station or the HVO commander, did they too, on certain occasions, make such individual decisions rather like the ones you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about that, but not before the second half of July. In Glavaticevo, there was a MUP unit, a formation, company size, and my friend, Mr. Nusret Sacibovic was in it. He was a member of the military investigations commission. He was a lawyer. Unfortunately, he, too, is no longer among the living. He told me some details about these interventions made on the basis of family ties and certain persons of authority, so that some Serbs detained in Celebici were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, you said that your intervention in connection with Miro Golubovic was linked to the heightened anti-Serb feelings in town. Within the framework of your duties, did you ever learn that in the prison itself there were some mistreatment of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Cerovac, ever receive any reports, personally or your headquarters as such, that any illegal action was being taken against prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, as a member of the staff and of the joint command, did you ever learn of the conditions regarding the food for prisoners in Celebici differed from the food received by your own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. The situation with food for all defence elements, both the Territorial Defence and the troops of the HVO and the refugees who were in collective centres, the food was prepared in a central kitchen. The preparation of food was done centrally, was centralised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, with the exception of this general information, because these were not your responsibilities and the authority you granted on the basis of some intervention by individuals, did you later learn about what happened to the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the supreme command had issued a request for speeding up the work of the military investigations commission with the prisoners, and we, the TO staff, sent a questionnaire. We, in Konjic, did not have a developed judicial network. That was not our competence. I think there was some contacts. Was it in connection with the prisoners, these prisoners of war, to go to Mostar, but in view of the circumstances in Mostar and the development of operations, they could not be taken there safely. So it was decided, as far as I recall, that they should go to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the prison was, in fact, moved to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Communications, that is, the roads leading to Zenica by October and November, they were intercepted because of the conflict between the BiH army and the HVO, so this made difficult moving the prison. I wish to add that already at the beginning of November and in the course of November, I took over the duties of brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, you just said that you became brigade commander. Tell me, please, were the brigades the next stage in the development of Territorial Defence in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The development of the army, with all due respect, Madam Residovic, was conditioned by the further transformation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please be brief. You have shown us the chart with the formations. Tell us, please, how did the further development of the army in Konjic develop? After the detachments, what was the next stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We already have the evidence of General Arif on this point. The municipal staff became part of this course. You said about the winding up of this Celebici detention camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the late Arif Pasalic testified before this court that he knew what happened in November. I'm now asking this witness after the detachments came the brigades and the witness became a brigade commander. I'm asking him to tell us what General Pasalic could not confirm in court. If this witness can do it, I'm asking him to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have the chart with the detachments, and then please tell me, were brigades formed in Konjic and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Within the territory of Konjic municipality, two brigades were formed, the 45th brigade and the 7th brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What post did you hold in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When were these brigades formed? Where were the brigades formed?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When were the brigades formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The brigades were formed after the establishment of the fourth corps, which was established by decision of the presidency, so the decision on the formation of the corps as the command. Immediately after that came the agreements and the arrangements regarding the formation of brigades. This was the period of the transformation of the army throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The corps were formed for the first time and the other formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zejnil Delalic, at any point in time, have a command military position in any of the newly formed brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know when the prison in Celebici ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This occurred, I don't know exactly when, but I know that the prisoners were transferred to the sports hall in the area of town known as Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that time on, when the prisoners were brought to Celebici, that is, from May until that moment at the end of 1992 when they were transferred from Celebici to Musala, those who remained, can you tell me whether the municipal staff or the joint command ever gave any authorisation to Zejnil Delalic with respect to the barracks or to the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in that period, did the municipal staff or the joint command ever authorise Zejnil Delalic to appoint certain persons within the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your testimony, I would ask you only additionally when the last units of the Yugoslav People's Army left the town of Konjic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first half of the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Cerovac, in view of the fact that you explained to us the development of Territorial Defence in Konjic, were there ever any private armies in Konjic, outside these military structures that you have explained to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I think you said "private armies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must be talking about volunteers, not private armies. There was HOS. They were volunteers. They were not private armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, we heard testimony that HOS came in mid-August and that it was subordinated to the staff. I'm asking the witness because one witness said that there were private armies, and you heard the witness laugh at that, but that is why I'm asking whether there were any private armies or was there the Territorial Defence, the HVO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the existence of private armies in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In '92, do you know whether there were any Green Beret detachments in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In '92, did detachments --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did detachments of Green Berets exist or were they all under the command of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All units were under the command of the Territorial Defence. All the formations that we formed in the form of detachments. That was clear. I can't see --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did later any kind of association come into existence under that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as an association of citizens, the organisations under the Green Beret of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was in '94. In '94.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, thank you very much. I appreciate your willingness to come and testify before this court, especially in view of your impaired health.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completed the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination by defence lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The defence of Zdravko Mucic has no additional cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have this many questions of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The answers will probably be 50 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I hope not, Judge. Let me plug myself in and see if we can...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Let me reintroduce myself. My name is Tom Moran, and just so we're up front with everybody, you and I talked over the noon hour a little bit. Are we coming through in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, good. I'm going to direct your attention to a couple of things, one of which we talked about over the noon hour and to a couple of things you testified to on direct. Sir, you look tired and if, at any time, you don't understand me or if you're feeling ill or something like that, let me know. We'll stop. We'll work with you. If you don't understand one of my questions, stop me and I'll rephrase it. I'd like to direct your attention to some testimony you gave this morning on direct. You were talking about orders from the joint command at the time you were the operations officer. As I recall your testimony, it was that they had to be signed by both the commander of the TO and the commander of the HVO, who was the chief of staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You also said that if the commander was not there, he could specifically authorise you or some other member of the staff to sign his name to a specific order. You're nodding your head "yes," and this lady over here in the yellow outfit is what's called a court reporter. She has to write down everything that we say so that six months from now I can remember what you said. You also, as I recall, testified that the commander could authorise you orally to sign certain orders on his behalf. He could say at the morning briefing, I'm going off someplace. You can sign this order." Do you remember testifying to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I understood from our conversation during the lunch break that you used to be a professional soldier. And in all armies in the world, orders can be made, orders may be made orally or in writing. There are specific circumstances when orders, instructions or various authorisations are made orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I was getting at, though, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel was not disagreeing with you. He was merely reminding you of what you said. I think that was sufficient. You could have just said yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, he already said that the commander cannot have the next man to sign on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Coming right to the heart of the matter that I wanted to get at, is the reason you had to have commander Ramic's authority or issue an order on his behalf, while you were the operations officer, because only the commander has the right to give commands and give orders, and the only time that you as a non-commander can give orders is when you are specifically authorised by the commander to give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively, by authority of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was exactly the question I was asking, sir. Well, you've also been a commander and in the army that I was in, commanders were very special people. They could, for instance, punish their subordinates, punish soldiers, where someone who was not a commander was not. Was that the same way in the Bosnian army, only the commander could punish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, one more thing and then I think I'm through, judge. It wasn't 50 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You're not a lawyer, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There's too many of us. If someone were to ask you about some technical definitions in the Geneva convention. Let me give me a hard core example. If Ms. McHenry who is sitting over there, one of the prosecutors, were to ask you a technical question about a definition in the Geneva conventions, you wouldn't know the answer to that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of my training at studies in Sarajevo, I had an examination which was called international war law, and if you ask me a definition of a war crime, I can give it to you immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But, if she, for instance, were to ask you who was a protected person under the Geneva convention on civilians, you couldn't answer that question, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then if she asks it, you're more than welcome to answer it, if you think you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't tempt him more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I've gone as far as I wanted to go down this path. I afraid I may regret having done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, it is beyond --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I used to do that and none of my students could answer, technically, those questions. If the Yugoslav army can, if he can answer it, then he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. My name is Teresa McHenry and I'm going to be asking you some questions. If you don't understand a question, please tell me and I will repeat it or rephrase it. Sir, I'm going to have to ask that you speak into the microphone so that your answers can be recorded. Did you understand, that if you don't understand a question, you just have to let me know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Nodding will not suffice. You have to say yes or no because it has to be recorded. Nodding will not suffice, would not be sufficient. You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree that in April and May of 1992, Mr. Delalic was already functioning as a member of the TO, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Your statement is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When did Mr. Delalic start functioning as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military duty as member of the TO was during the 27th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that when Mr. Delalic took charge in liberating the Celebici barracks, he did so in his military capacity as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the military sense, in the logistic sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you previously gave a statement to a representative from the Defence, didn't you, on the 22nd of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only once did I give a statement to The Hague Tribunal, and after that, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You were examined by the Defence attorney before you came here? You were examined by one of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour. The interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She's referring to that statement which you made to one of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that in your prior statement, you stated that: "I know that after a meeting, Zejnil Delalic joined the patriotic movement and as a member of the Territorial Defence, without any function, took part with us in liberating the former JNA compound in the Celebici barracks." You would agree you made that statement, wouldn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there as an ordinary volunteer, but formally he was not. He did not belong to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, my question is would you agree with me that previously you stated that when Mr. Delalic participated in the liberation of the Celebici barracks, he did so as a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as a member of the Territorial Defence. I was at the head of the group of people who are members of the TO, and I explained my tasks very clearly. We were all in uniforms and armed and Mr. Delalic performed voluntary functions on a logistic basis. He provided for the accommodations and did some physical work, the loading and unloading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delalic in uniform and armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw Dr. Delalic in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In uniform, well, I saw him when we were sending off the unit, which we sent to the area of Pazaric and tactical area 1. It was a solemn occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And Mr. Delalic was wearing a uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was this the first time you had ever seen Mr. Delalic in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, Your Honour, that this was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was that the first time you had ever seen Mr. Delalic in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time, the first time someone wears a uniform does not necessarily mean that he's a member of the TO. To wear any part of the uniform, if a young person was wearing it or someone who was not able to be in the military, well, this was a specific atmosphere prevailing then. I don't know if you will be able to grasp this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, after this time -- let me ask you: Before you saw Mr. Delalic at the solemn occasion of the Gajret unit, how many times in the month previous to that, from May 15 to June 15th, how many times had you seen Mr. Delalic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? Do you mean from May 15th to June 15th?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From May 15th to June 15th, on approximately how many occasions did you see Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say even approximately. I cannot pronounce myself on this subject. I cannot really say how many times I would have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it more or less than ten times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you think it's fair if he says he cannot remember, that's all he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could it have been the first time you saw Dr. Delalic was on June 15th during the Gajret unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he met him when they took over the possession of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Between the time that you took over the Celebici barracks with Mr. Delalic, in the time you saw him on the solemn occasion, did you see Mr. Delalic in between those times or you have just no idea if you ever saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to correct something. The first time, it was not the 15th of June but the 20th of June. The 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, between the time that you took over the Celebici barracks with Mr. Delalic and the 20th of June, during the solemn occasion of the Gajret, do you know whether or not you saw Mr. Delalic at all during that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say the number of times I saw him. I would like to speak the truth. If I had known that I had seen him five times, I would say so. If I had known if I saw him ten times, I would have so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I understand that you don't remember the exact number of times. I am asking you whether or not there were any times between the time you took over the Celebici barracks and the 20th of June that you saw Mr. Delalic. Did you see him even on one time or you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of my answers, as far as I can recollect, I said that I had contacts with Mr. Delalic before he travelled to the Republic of Croatia, in his apartment. And if you want to know how he was dressed, I can tell you that. I outline this briefly, if I asked him if he were able to provide some supplies to us. Actually he was dressed very simply, he was wearing a robe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask for the usher's assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 239.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this as the copy of the statement you gave to the Defence in June of 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the end of the statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to direct your attention to the eighth paragraph, it's a paragraph that begins, "I know that after the meeting, Zejnil Delalic joined the patriotic movement and as a member of the Territorial Defence". Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you now agree with me that in your prior statement, you indicated that when Mr. Delalic took part in liberating the Celebici barracks, he did so as a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I quoted that in the first time I read it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what his statement is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'll ask him to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has answered this question twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I didn't see any discrepancy between what he said here and what is in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You don't go about asking questions when they are clear. I don't think anybody does it. You read it again. Read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that when Mr. Delalic participated with you in liberating the Celebici barracks, although he did not have a function, he did so as a member of a Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This question has also been answered by the witness, so I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the Territorial Defence, not in the capacity of a soldier, nor as a soldier having a specific duty. What he did, he did out of patriotic reasons with respect to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, can you explain what it means here when it says, "As a member of the Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you are insisting on this. He has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is he doing at the TO then? He said without any functions. He went with the team. He was living on logistics. That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that there's some question about whether or not he was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then he must have some function as a soldier, as a bureaucrat, as a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's why I am asking the witness to explain what he means when he says, "As a member of the Territorial Defence".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you please explain to me what you mean when you say, "As a member of the Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Read the whole statement, everything on it. What does it say? Read the whole statement. I have read the whole statement. Maybe it's a misquote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask the question again. And what he means by as a member of the deal without any functions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir what do you mean when you say, "As member of the Territorial Defence without any function"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, at the time, all we had developed organisational structure of the detachments and of the units and the personnel body of the -- had knowledge of this. And nowhere, Mr. Delalic figured in the documents, neither in the staff, nor in the units or the detachments were subordinated to the staff, so nowhere as a member of the Territorial Defence. I am just pointing out that he was performing a patriotic duty and obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me move on. Sir, you testified about the war presidency, would you agree with me that in order to organise better the Territorial Defence units in Konjic, the war presidency made frequent staff changes, including changing the Territorial Defence commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, the war presidency did not carry out such changes. These changes carried out by the municipal parliament of Konjic within the framework of its responsibilities and it, in fact, proposed, but appointments, but actual appointments were made in Sarajevo. During the war, the war presidency, which is a civilian body, which functioned because the municipal assembly was not able to function. I would not refer to it as a war presidency. It had authority that is of the municipal assembly. It could not carry out changes. It could only make proposals and not carry out changes because, otherwise, there would be an interference of competency, of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case -- well, let me just go on. Now, you would agree with me, sir, that when Mr. Ramic was appointed TO commander in May and then again appointed TO commander in the beginning of June, there was never ever written communication from Sarajevo, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Written appointments, to be able to come from Sarajevo, you have to understand the communication problems we had between Konjic and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just tell you that sometimes if you can just answer the question "yes or no", an explanation may not be necessary, I may just be asking you to confirm something and an explanation may not be necessary. So if it's the case that written appointments of TO commanders were not made by Sarajevo, all you have to do is say "yes" and I think we'll be finished more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have to tell you, Mr. Ramic performed a function. He was appointed and they do have those documents, but those documents could not reach us in time for the appointments because of the circumstances I wanted to tell you about. In any case, his function of commander was a legal function and there's -- there is nothing debatable about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me then ask you then, is it correct, sir, that you have never seen any written appointment from Mr. Ramic as TO commander in May at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see them for these reasons, but I did see the appointments personally and they must be somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that in the prior statement to the Defence, you stated in order to organise better the Territorial Defence units in Konjic's municipality, the war presidency of the Konjic's municipal assembly made frequent staff changes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let me ask that you look at the fourth paragraph of your statement which states at the time this begins, at the time of the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the third sentence, sir, do you agree with me, sir, that your statement states in order to organise better, the Territorial Defence units in Konjic's municipality, the war presidency of the Konjic municipal assembly made frequent staff changes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think my colleague did not understand me well. I am just telling you -- I am telling you again again, those authorisations of the municipal assembly, I started working in '87 in the municipal staff and I know what exactly are the competencies of the municipal assembly, which were passed on. The municipal assembly did this in the 70s, in the 60s, in the 80s and the 90s. It is the only one that is authorised to nominate commanders of the TO staff. To add a brief CV and this sent to the republican staff in the Sarajevo or the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which carries out the actual appointments in accordance with its competencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will counsel kindly indicate what is the inference of that sentence? Why this question is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, his statement said something different from what he stated in his testimony, and so I was trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What he says, and I think it's legitimate, in order to organise better TO units in Konjic, the war presidency of Konjic municipal assembly may request changes. So I didn't think anything wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not saying that that's not correct. In fact, they did make frequent staff changes, but the witness has just said that it's not correct. In fact, he's stated that the person to whom he gave his statement must have written it down incorrectly because it does differ from his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I really don't see the need for this caution because no problems staff changes here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'll move on. I believe he's stated -- he's given his explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, when Mr. Delalic was appointed by the war presidency of coordinator, you would agree with me that it was to remove or resolve the differences between the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delalic appointed liaison officer by the war presidency to remove or resolve the differences between the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could be called liaison officer figuratively, but it doesn't mean anything. His role was clearly stated by the legal authorities of Konjic's municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in May of 1992, did you see the appointment of Mr. Delalic's coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And when did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my return from an artillery position at Lakuica (phoen). I had learned that joint command had been formed and that in that command I had been appointed operations officer and this was around the 19th or the 20th. I wasn't there at any joint meeting between the legal organs of authority and the military bodies. That is, the TO, the HVO and the MUP. But the function of coordinator, a decision taken by the war presidency to that effect, I did see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree with me that in your prior statement, you stated that Mr. Delalic was appointed coordinator or liaison officer, among other things, to remove the differences between the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, liaison officer, I use the term figuratively, but this lady Seken Ragita (phoen), added that I wish to underline that I used it figuratively to explain it to her. But, in fact, Zejnil Delalic did not that have that function. He was not authorised as a coordinator to remove any disagreements. And these disagreements were -- occurred frequently. For instance, logistic requirements were made by a representative of the HVO, the TO, the civilian authorities had their own very wide range of difficult problems, refugees, food supplies, shelter for the population, provision of accommodation for the refugees, so that the civilian authorities had these problems to deal with. On the other hand, there were representatives of the TO with their own demands, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we'll have a break and assemble at four-thirty, thirty minutes time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he's still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if, in describing his various duties as coordinator, Mr. Delalic said, among other things, he was involved in resolving personnel matters between the HVO and the TO, would that be consistent with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Delalic never had such authority to deal with personnel problems between the TO and the HVO, nor any other disagreements. His function was purely a function of coordination between the legal authorities and the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just to make sure I understand, in your prior statement when you talk about Mr. Delalic's appointment as one that was done to remove disputes, are you saying that the Defence representative wrote down what you said incorrectly or just that you misspoke when you said it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, especially the first part of the question? What person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, immediately before the break, you had looked at your statement and the discussion of where it is reported that what you said was that Mr. Delalic was appointed as coordinator or as liaison officer to remove the disputes between the TO and the HVO. I know you've explained what you now believe to be the correct position, but my question is: Do you agree that you said this in your statement to the Defence in June '96 or is it your position that you said something different and she wrote it down wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to draw attention to the fact that this is not being read properly because the word used is "differences," rather than "disputes" because the witness did not, in fact, say that in his previous statement. The word used is "differences."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I stand corrected. In my understanding, they are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, is it your question that he should understand what is stated as different from what he told the person who wrote it down?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he has testified to something different than what's in the statement, and I've asked him about that, and he has given me a long answer, and I don't understand if his answer is saying that the person wrote it down wrong or if, in fact, he said it, but is now just saying that it's really not a correct description of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you would kindly be a little more helpful to the Trial Chamber, let's hear your proper formulation of what you think he said at that time and what he now says it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that the recordation of your prior statement talks about, and I'm referring to the paragraph that's in the middle of the second page approximately, that says: "I also know that Zejnil Delalic was on a decision of the Konjic municipal war presidency, appointed coordinator between the presidency and the Konjic municipality defence forces." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And it then goes on to say: "The defence forces were composed of two components, the Territorial Defence and the HVO, and had separate systems of command and control. It was evident even then that there were differences in the HVO concept of defence against the aggression. In order to set up a better system of defence and remove such differences, Zejnil Delalic was appointed liaison officer." It then goes on to say: "At a meeting between representatives of the HVO and the Territorial Defence, held on the 20th of May, Mr. Zejnil Delalic acquainted us with the paper concerning his appointment to the post, so afterwards, any problems with respect to that coordination we resolved with Zejnil Delalic." My question is, sir, do you agree that this is what you said previously?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think it's better you leave him to deal with it? Would you kindly give your attention, I'm sure you can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part of the text in which I say that, by decision of the war presidency, the position of coordinator was established, and I said quite correctly what the coordination was, that is, between the civilian organs of authority and the defence forces. That is correct. The second part of your citation linked to differences in terms of control and command, and the disagreements that existed, I should like to explain as follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you can explain, but first before you explain, can we just clarify, did you say this when you gave your statement to the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part is accurate, but a moment ago, I said that Ms. Senka Nojica didn't understand me then. She didn't fully understand what I was saying. This was in 1996. I have come here exclusively to present to you the truth and to present the evidence for you to be able to make relevant conclusions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you believe, that she wrote down what you said, incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'm now going to go on. Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what he's saying is that what was written down might have been what was thought as truth, but from the explanation he was giving us, if what is meant is differences in the concept of defence, it could not be. This is what he was trying to explain to us, that Delalic could not have been the liaison officer in respect of that type of differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I was offering his prior statement for impeachment, merely for purposes of Your Honours determining his credibility, and you have heard his explanation and you have the document. So you may make your own evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, when shown a document by Ms. Residovic concerning the railroad, a document signed by Mr. Delalic and others, you indicated that Mr. Delalic had been given a certain task regarding the railroad; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the proposal of the economic staff to establish rail communication together with the representatives of the management of the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat it. I'm just trying to remind you of the general subject matter so that you will understand my next question. You don't have to repeat what you have already said. If you remember that, all you have to do is say, "Yes, I remember." All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your concrete question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is: Who exactly had given Mr. Delalic the task regarding the railroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The economic staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is this the economic staff, is this a part of the war presidency or the joint command or the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of the organs of authority formed by the legal authorities to deal with the civilian segment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So it was not any part of the TO or the joint command; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just go on. In addition to this document, I assume that you saw other orders that were also signed by Mr. Delalic as coordinator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question before I see those documents. After all, it is 1998 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask that you be shown documents, Prosecution Exhibits 210 and 213. Let me ask while we're getting those documents, because it may not even be necessary for you to look at them, sir. Even if you don't remember the specifics, would you agree with me that there were some orders signed by Mr. Delalic that did not involve logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you remember, did you see documents in 1992 signed by Mr. Delalic in his role as coordinator, that did not have to do with logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If any documents were signed by him, on which the function was indicated, the function of commander, then Zejnil Delalic was probably a witness to an agreement which he needed to coordinate the relationship between the civilian authorities and the military in connection with our needs regarding some specific material. And if he signed, then he signed only as an agreement and not as somebody having the authority to give orders to members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go on, sir. Sir, am I correct that in the joint command staff, you were officer for operations in training and at the same time, in the TO staff, you were chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So in addition to the joint command staff, there was a separate TO staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To ensure the better functioning of the defence forces of the municipality of Konjic, we attempted, through a joint command, to unify these two components of the armed forces, to improve our organisation and to be more successful in resisting the aggression. Two systems which comprise the joint command were the Territorial Defence and the Croatian defence council, both systems had separate systems of control and command, along vertical lines. May I explain this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think you already explained it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The answer was simple. You could have said yes. You don't have to give extra explanations when there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that the set-up of the joint command was not something envisioned in the regulations of the Bosnian army, it was something that Konjic did to try to solve the unusual and difficult situation it was in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a specific decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think what counsel is suggesting, that device was improvised to meet the difficulties of the situation which faced you. The situation of the joint command was the advice to meet the specific situation which confronted you at that time, not necessarily the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The army was one, but one took its instructions from Grude and the other took its instructions from Sarajevo. In order to have joint operations, you have one joint command. This is what she's saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully agree with what you have just said. That is exactly true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified there were occasions, even extended occasions, when the appointed TO commander was gone and you functioned as the TO commander in his absence. You testified that one of those occasions was during the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: During the Oganj operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Approximately, sir, when were the other occasions when you functioned as the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When commander Ramic was wounded at Prenj, Mount Prenj. He personally told me, due to specific circumstances, that I should take over command. Of course, at the time when this oral authorisation was given to me, because we had communications through links, he didn't tell me he was wounded and this was logical because that would be counterproductive for our forces as we could be overheard by the enemy. So I learned that later and this is only logical during combat, when a commander is wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You need to answer the question. When the Oganj operations started. You acted as a commander. Was there any other occasion when you acted as commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Oganj Operation started, the commander was Mr. Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was there any other occasion when you acted as commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the Oganj Operation, 15 or 16 days later, when he was wounded, I took over, upon his orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there any other time, besides during the second part of July during the Oganj Operation, was there any other occasion where you functioned as TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. During the Oganj Operation, when you were functioning as TO commander, who functioned as your chief of staff, if any one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one. No one could because we were in a specific situation. There was a war and we were not officers in offices. There were my friends getting killed around me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that Mr. Goran Lokas was part of the security division of the joint command. You also, I believe, indicated that Mr. Sacir Pajic was part of the security of the joint command, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Sacir Pajic was also part of the TO command, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, when asked about who took over Mr. Goran Lokas's function in the beginning of June when he left, you talked about a Mr. Kostic. Is it your testimony that Mr. Kostic took over the position of Mr. Lokas or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position of chief of security in the joint command was allotted to the Croatian Defence Council. So as I saw Elvir Kostic there, who was a former officer in the state security service, that he held that position. No appointment was made by, conditionally speaking, the TO to that position because that position, according to the distribution of posts in the joint command, was allotted to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was the position filled by the joint command? Was there ever any discussion in the joint command, of which you were a member, about the need to fill this position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kostic attend meetings of the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meetings that I attended were attended by the following people or, rather, the people holding the following positions: The commander, the logistics officer, the chief of staff of the joint command. From the security sector, rarely would somebody participate at meetings having to do with some arrangements, agreements, et cetera, especially Mr. Lokas, because he spent very little of his time in the premises of the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, is it a fair statement that you don't know about the authority of persons who had duties in the joint command or the TO command, that had duties that were unrelated to your own duties?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the question is such that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It relates to one of the maps which you produced in which he has drawn the various functions in the joint command. She's questioning with regard to that, whether -- it is in regard to that question, the map, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it a fair statement that you don't know about the authority of other persons in the command staff who had duties that were unrelated to your own duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The duties depended on the positions. That is clear. The name of the function is quite clear. Assistant commander for logistics is responsible for logistics. The head of the security sector deals with security; intelligence with intelligence; the operations sector, the operations. That is the only answer I can give you as a military man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: With regard to what you're saying, would you regard it as fair if anyone made a comment that any persons whose duties are not related to yours may not be familiar to you? That you may not be familiar with the duties of those who are not related to your own duties, even though they are in the chart and you have so described them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking about the chart, I know the theory of it, the jurisdiction of those positions. During my work in the joint command, I didn't know what they were doing on a daily basis because there was no obligation for them to brief me about those things, according to the control and command structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe knowing the administrative set-up, but not the person who were actually performing those functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me, sir, for instance, that your chart doesn't have Mr. Kostic even on the chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic is not on the chart, but his sector is on the chart, the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you've stated that during the Borci Operation, Mr. Delalic was functioning in a military capacity as a soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything I said about Mr. Delalic during the Borci Operation, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me, sir, that when the Borci Operation was being planned, Mr. Delalic was involved in his function as a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I will not agree with you. Mr. Delalic does not have military and technical knowledge to plan an action such as Borci. This is a very serious exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not even as a logistics officer? Not even as a person responsible for logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even as a person involved in logistics, but Mr. Kevric was present there on matters of logistics. Mr. Delalic was requested to perform a military role, not to issue orders, but to carry on a military function, given his abilities to help us in the logistic security area, because the situation was specific in terms of the terrain and communication links, and to convey requests from Glavaticevo to Konjic and establish contact with the local population for transporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that in his function as coordinator, including coordinating between the war presidency and the Defence forces, Mr. Delalic was at least knowledgeable about the operation in Borci being planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, through Mr. Delalic, we established contacts vis-à-vis the authorities concerning a number of needs. The needs related to the provision of first aid equipment, transport conveyance, and needs which could be provided by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree that the order that you referred to signed by Mr. Ramic about the Borci operation, one copy was sent to Mr. Delalic and another copy was sent to the war presidency? Would you agree with that? If you need to see the order to answer that question, we can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't need to see the order. I would like to only say that it is quite normal that on the basis of a written document, we inform the civilian authorities what our intentions are and also the coordinator what our intentions were, because we cannot say in a figurative sense, "We need this and that." We must explain why we need all this because we are a poor town and we cannot just ask for anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you will also agree with me that in Mr. Ramic's order for Borci operations, he gives certain orders to the MUP units, to the MUP units that were going to participate in the operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it really relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the fact that orders were being given to the MUP units by the TO commander is relevant to, in general, showing the complexity and the intermixing of all the various parts of the defence forces in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: MUP also had some combat units, and from Borci, after the HVO -- particularly, after the HVO withdrew, they needed to collect all the forces available to make the operation successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right. If this witness agrees that under certain circumstances the TO commander had authority to give orders to the MUP, I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe the MUP representative attended the meeting where it was decided to have this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe, but if what this witness says is correct, it would still be unusual and, in fact, not possible for Mr. Ramic to give orders to the MUP unit, so I am just finding that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree with me that there were certain occasions, including for the Borci operation, when Mr. Ramic gave orders to MUP units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not illogical. I would contact the Devil himself to save my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you talked about Tactical Group 1. In 1992, did you, yourself, ever see any order or orders appointing Mr. Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
